newsitem.title: LEBANON: Saudi buys Lebanon's biggest bank network.
newsitem.headline: Saudi buys Lebanon's biggest bank network.

text.p: Lebanon's central bank said on Thursday it had agreed to sell Credit Libanais, a medium-size bank with the biggest retail banking network in the country, to Saudi billionaire Khalid bin Mahfouz for $163 million.
The purchase gave the billionaire sheikh, who last year took over Saudi Arabia's biggest bank, National Commercial Bank (NCB), a network of 44 branches in Lebanon and a Cyprus Offshore Banking Unit.
Beirut bankers said the deal added a major new competitor to Lebanon's crowded banking sector.

"This is foreign competition in the true sense of the word," said Joe Sarrouh, executive adviser to the chairman of Fransabank, a leading Beirut bank. "Other foreign banks in the country have a limited presence."
Several foreign banks operate in Lebanon but they are currently restricted to a single branch.
Bank of Lebanon Governor Riad Salameh told Reuters the total value of the deal was $163 million.

CL is a commercial and investment bank with an extensive credit card business and a 3.43 percent market share. Assets were $898 million at end-1996 -- 10th in the sector. Shareholders' equity was eighth at $66 million but profits ranked 24th at $3.55 million.

The central bank, which acquired 97 percent of CL's shares after a financial crash in 1989, announced in May it had decided to sell its stake by private placement. Salameh said several bids were received, mainly from Arab and Lebanese investors.
Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz's bid was the highest, he said.
However, this was not the only reason for the deal. Salameh said it would bring Lebanon the added benefit of strategically linking it with the Saudi banking sector.
"This (sale) is going to be a very efficient tool for bringing together the banking and financial markets in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon," he said in a telephone interview.
At least two Lebanese banks were rumoured to have been interested in acquiring Credit Libanais and Sarrouh expressed some disappointment that it went to a non-Lebanese.
"We would have preferred a Lebanese bank to get it as an acquisition and merger, to encourage other banks in the sector to merge," Sarrouh told Reuters.
However, under the terms of the central bank's offer the purchaser must operate CL as a separate entity for at least a year, Sarrouh said.

"In my opinion it would have been very interesting if a merger had been allowed from day one, if the negotiations had been for a merger rather than for a sale under which CL had to stand alone," Sarrouh added.

He said a merger deal would have set a precedent for banks on handling the thorny issue of staff in mergers, which have failed to take place despite a widely perceived need for the banking industry to rationalise and develop.

Some Beirut bankers say the central bank carried out no rationalisation of CL's 750-strong staff during its tenure. They say the staff issue could be problematic for prospective mergers at a time when labour and politicians are warning of social problems in the country.
Salameh told Reuters the central bank understood that Khalid bin Mahfouz would maintain CL's current staff and products.
Sarrouh said the sale of CL was a challenge for Lebanon's banks and with Khalid bin Mahfouz and Saudi Arabia's National Commercial Bank behind it CL would provide healthy competition.
"This may be healthy in inciting local banks to develop consumer products at a faster pace," he said.
"I think it is a challenge. They are a big and expert bank with multiple activities. They will add a special flavour to the competition in the country," Sarrouh said.
